subsubtopic: PROPOSED PROHIBITION OF THE PASSAGE OF TANKERS THROUGH GEORGIAN BAY DURING WINTER-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. I have been a member of this House for four years and have never risen under Standing Order 43 before now because in most cases I feel the motions do not accomplish very much. However, in this particular case I think this matter is very important.
On December 23 of last year a large oil tanker spill occurred covering some 50,000 plus miles of the shoreline of Georgian Bay, and the many islands there. In view of past representations to the Ministry of Transport and a recent petition to the Prime Minister containing over 2,000 names which he personally received, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis):
That this House direct the federal government to prohibit the winter passage of oil and gasoline tankers through Georgian Bay so that the potential environmental and economic disaster which would arise from a spill of greater magnitude may be prevented.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that almost two months have elapsed since I brought certain difficulties to the attention of the government with respect to Loto Canada, and in view of the fact that investigations by the police into both Loto Canada and its predecessor have not yet
prompted any official response by the government, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity arising out of information on CBC news this morning that the drilling blowout last summer which occurred in the Beaufort Sea came about as a result of eased requirements on the drilling procedures granted to Dome Petroleum.
Given the risks involved in the project as proposed, given that the amended drilling procedures were authorized without reference to the minister responsible, that the accident caused the death of one man and serious injury to another and that this information was not available at the time of the inquest into the accident, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That this matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development and that the committee be asked to investigate this serious accident.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the dairy farmers of Canada have made that representation to us, as have some of the provincial governments through their provincial marketing boards. speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON APPOINTMENT AND EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the House of recent developments respecting appointments and employment practices in the public service. You may recall our discussions here on December 9 and 10, 1976, concerning allegations of improper staffing action. I have been advised that the Public Service Commission has taken the matter in hand and that the chairman of the commission has made a public statement. I should like to table his response and, on behalf of the Prime Minister, indicate his support of it. I firmly believe our federal public service ranks high on the list of federal public services in western democratic countries.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON APPOINTMENT AND EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON APPOINTMENT AND EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
We have been fortunate, indeed, to attract the large number of qualified public servants we have in the service today and their dedication and loyalty is to be commended.
As members of this House know, it has been nearly ten years since the Public Service Employment Act, the Public Service Staff Relations Act and the revised Financial Administration Act were passed by the House. In recognition of the need for a review of this situation, the government asked Dr. Finkelman to undertake an examination of the Public Service Staff Relations Act and its administration and to make recommendations having regard to the experience gained since that act came into force, and how it should be amended or revised adequately to meet the needs of the employer and employee in the public service and the employee organizations that represent them and to serve the interests of the public. That report was the subject of consideration at a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Employer and Employee Relations.
The government intends to introduce amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act based on the recommendations of the Finkelman and parliamentary reports. In this context it would also introduce amendments to the Public Service Employment Act and the Financial Administration Act.
As announced by my predecessor in May, 1976, the government will establish a review body to examine staffing, appoint-
February 4, 1977

merits and training in the public service. I am pleased to announce that following consultation with the parties concerned, the terms of reference of a special committee on the review of personnel management and the merit principle has been agreed to.
This committee will examine all matters pertaining to the Public Service Employment Act with particular reference to (a) the merit principle and its application as it relates to initial appointment, internal appointment and promotion and eligibility of public servants to participate in competitions; (b) access to employment with respect to training; (c) process of appeal and redress relating to appointment problems and demotion; (d) scope of collective bargaining as it applies to (a), (b) and (c); (e) operation and assistance in the operation of training and development programs; (f) fostering of improved employee-employer relations; and (g) more efficient personnel management systems taking into account operational needs of departments and the need to provide an efficient and effective service to the public.
At the request of the unions, and upon mutual agreement by all affected parties, the first phase of the review will involve a separate examination by each side of the above-mentioned issues. Following a suitable period for these two exercises, the special committee, composed of a chairman and a representative of the government and a representative chosen by the unions, will begin meeting, leading to the preparation of a public report.
An announcement of the membership of the special committee will be made at a later date. Where it is possible to reach agreement, recommendations will be made to the government. In areas where no agreement is possible, the chairman will identify the different points of view and will be free to make his opinion known as to what options should be considered. During the deliberations of the committee there will be consultation between the government and the unions and between other interested individuals and organizations, particularly the Public Service Commission. While the committee will be examining roles and relationships, it will not be asked to make recommendations concerning organizational structures.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON APPOINTMENT AND EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the traditional way I wish to thank the President of the Privy Council for forwarding an advance copy of the statement to me. I also wish to join the minister in paying tribute to the public service of Canada which I have reason to believe, from experience and for other reasons, ranks high among public services in the western world. It is a fine service, but I am afraid the admission today that a special committee is to be set up to examine some very important matters suggests that, fine as it is, it is in a state of some uncertainty as to its general acceptance by the government.
One of the matters raised in this statement is the proposed amendment to the Public Service Staff Relations Act. We heard about this from the former president of the privy council, so this is the second time we have heard of it. It sounds as though we are putting up the banns for marriage.
Public Service
Will there be a third statement before the amendments are introduced, or are they to be brought before us soon?
Speaking as a member of the committee which studied the Finkelman report and looked into employer-employee relations in the public service, I feel it is high time to bring that legislation before the House. I hope that this is not another stalling tactic on the part of the government, another delay in bringing forward the legislation. In general, we welcome the statement, although with reservations.
Unfortunately, the statement does not mention something else which also stemmed from the work of the joint committee on employer-employee relations in the public service. It says nothing about the need to examine the operation of the Public Service Commission within the ambit of the Public Service Staff Relations Act. If that question is to be the subject of further legislation or study remains to be seen. Regrettably, it was not raised in the statement.
The list of matters set out on page 2 of the statement which the committee is to examine is of prime importance to the public service and shows the degree to which the public service has fallen on evil days. As has been said more than once, public servants are uncertain about their future. Regrettably, there is a drop in the morale of the public service. The establishment of a special committee which is to study certain questions fundamental to the public service suggests to us that the government recognizes the demoralization of the public service. When I say this, I am thinking particularly of the merit principle, and promotion.
There are procedures for appealing decisions concerning promotion. One can take one's appeal to the federal court, if necessary. I have correspondence from the chairman of the Public Service Commission saying that few appeals have been taken to the federal court. But that fact, I suggest, is not an indication of the amount of discontent in the public service or the way in which appeals are being handled. I hope the committee that is to be established will look into these matters carefully.
I notice that subparagraph (0 on page 2 of the statement speaks of the "fostering of improved employer-employee relations." That language shows, I suggest, that the government recognizes something is wrong. I wonder if that "something wrong" is not spotlighted by the expression in the last paragraph on page 2 which reads in part, "the first phase of the review will involve a separate examination by each side-" Why by each side? Are we not all on the same side? When the public service was known as the civil service, it was on the same side; we were all on one side.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON APPOINTMENT AND EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON APPOINTMENT AND EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
It worked hand in glove with the government. Then there was no mention of the parties being on each side. That we have come to such a pass is regrettable. It is high time for the matters listed in the statement to be examined.

February 4, 1977
Public Service
Certain other questions ought to be taken into account. For example, the public service is demoralized partly because there are no standard conditions of work throughout the service. In one department the employees are entitled, say, to three weeks annual leave, whereas in other departments they could be entitled to more. Also, provision for sick leave is not standard across the board. I think all such questions should be treated in a standard way, so that each department will know it is being treated as all other departments are being treated.
Finally, I shall comment on the expression on page 3 of the statement reading, "Where it is possible to reach agreement, recommendations will be made to the government..." Since the statement speaks of the two sides in this matter, I suggest that if one side feels aggrieved, it should be able to make recommendations and have them considered. Any decision, including a rejection, if that is necessary, ought to be handed down with reasons. Although we welcome this particular statement as an indication that the government intends to improve the morale of the public service, we have some reservations about it.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON APPOINTMENT AND EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was particularly pleased to hear the President of the Privy Council in the early part of his remarks use these words: "We have been fortunate indeed to attract the large number of qualified public servants we have in the service today and their dedication and loyalty is to be commended."
I was also pleased to note that at that point the House applauded. It was interesting to hear a comment like that, following some of the other things which have been said in this House in recent weeks about the loyalty and reliability of some of our public servants. We have also heard members in this House, even on the government side, indulging in the pastime of sniping at public servants and blaming them for the faults of the government. I think that once in a while it is good for the sort of thing the statement says to be expressed in the House, and for the House to applaud it.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON APPOINTMENT AND EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON APPOINTMENT AND EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES
speechtext: The fact is that we have a very good public service.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON APPOINTMENT AND EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Well said, Stanley.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON APPOINTMENT AND EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
It is inevitable that when very large numbers of people are involved, some mistakes will be made. However, in the main, we are well served. I am also interested to note that Mr. Gallant's statement, which the minister tabled at the same time, emphasizes the importance of protecting the merit principle. Mr. Gallant recognized in his statement that the delegation of hiring powers to the departments had created problems, but he affirmed in the statement that the Public Service Commission regards it as its job to make sure that the merit system is observed. Because there have been some questions about that point, this review is important.

Today in his statement the minister said that two things are to be done. First, as the minister announced, the government intends to introduce amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act, the Public Service Employment Act and the Financial Administration Act. All those acts have to do with the public service. Like the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich I hope those amendments will be forthcoming soon.
The second proposal concerns the establishment of the special three-person committee which is to study the matters the minister listed this morning. I am not horrified, as was my friend for Esquimalt-Saanich, at the suggestion that the representatives for either side in these discussions would have the chance before they meet to line up all the issues with which they are to deal. After all, it is a management-labour situation.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON APPOINTMENT AND EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
But it should not be; it
ought to be a service relationship.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON APPOINTMENT AND EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
One should be realistic in arrangements of this kind. The things to which special attention need to be given in the attempt to improve the work of the public service in the main fall under three headings. First, we must do everything possible to enhance and protect the merit system and see to it that all the changes which have been made have not chipped it away. Second, we must underline, confirm and widen the collective bargaining process. It is still my view that it should include such things as classifications, promotions, and so on. I believe that is in the review which is to be made.
In the third place it seems to me that more ought to be said and done about the pensions of our public servants. That I believe those pensions should be improved is well known. But I think the government should take a more aggressive stand in defence of our public servants and their pensions. I deplore, with everything within me, the sniping and attacking that is going on, based largely upon hypothetical situations and a few individual cases. Many public servants, retired and working, wish the government's voice would be heard with regard to this matter. If the government were a little more outspoken in defence of its public servants both working and retired, it would help to improve the morale in the service.
I am a little amazed at the suggestion that this committee will make no recommendations. I suppose if it has the right to express its opinions, that is really the same thing under another name. In any case, we welcome this display of interest in the good job being done by our public service and also the display of interest in improving it. We wish this committee well. We hope that before long we will see the legislation that has again been promised.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON APPOINTMENT AND EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to express my appreciation to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) for having had the courtesy of sending me his statement in French. One might say, Mr. Speaker, that it complies with the procedure-and I agree-
February 4, 1977

but still one must accept to do one's duty. That is why I congratulate him.
The president's statement deals first with appointment and hiring practices in the public service. Those practices are not widely known but I presume that every candidate for a position within the public service is fairly treated. Otherwise the President of the Privy Council is fully justified to consider amendments to the public service legislation. The President of the Privy Council has informed the House that he will set up a review body to examine staffing, appointments and training practices in the public service. In paragraph (g), page 2 of his statement, the minister said the committee will examine, and I quote:
(g) more efficient personnel management systems taking into account operational needs of departments and the need to provide an efficient and effective service to the public.
Mr. Speaker, I would not apply that criticism to civil servants generally because, on the whole, I agree with the President of the Privy Council that standards are quite good in the public service. Still, the fact remains that some civil servants should be reminded of their duties in the performance of their work if they are to lose their illusions of grandeur and quit behaving as if they owned the country.
I should like to draw the attention of the President of the Privy Council to the delays in some of the negotiations between the various levels of government, and to the fact that in some cases those delays can be blamed on the officials to whom the negotiations were entrusted. The public is becoming increasingly aware that officials are responsible for big policies and big decisions and that some of them could not care less about the authority of their minister. Such a behaviour encroaches upon the principles of administrative hierarchy.
I therefore hope that the nature of the measures mentioned in the statement of the President of the Privy Council are such that they will improve relations between employers and employees, and that every civil servant will be treated on merit without political considerations entering the picture. I know, on the other hand, that it is not easy to serve the public. Still, those who chose that vocation, the civil service or the political arena, should expect to be the target of some criticism. However, if in the space of two months the government has felt that it should draw the attention of the House to this matter, obviously there is some unrest. If creating that committee, and changing the public service legislation as the government suggests, can improve the situation, I am sure that is what everyone of us wishes.
So, under the circumstances, I feel that the government is making an effort to act; but, if there are complaints about administrative delays in the case of some officials, then the government will have to set the example by going ahead as soon as possible, since it has introduced those measures.

I should like briefly to explain my reason for introducing this bill. The commissioners recommended that the redistributed riding be known as Brampton-Halton Hills. subsubtopic: STUDY OF HEALTH CARE PRODUCTS SECTOR
speechtext: What are the terms of reference and what is the objective of the study of the health care products sector being undertaken by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce?

speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh Poulin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: STUDY OF HEALTH CARE PRODUCTS SECTOR
speechtext: In so far as the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is concerned: The health care product sector is one of growing importance to Canada, having the capacity to make a significant contribution to the government's objective of improving the quality of life for all Canadians. Canadian consumption of health care products, which include medical supplies, equipment and devices as well as pharmaceuticals, is now well in excess of one billion dollars, nearly half of which is imported. Growth in consumption of health care products has been above the average of that of manufactured products and it is expected to continue this way. The objective of the study now being undertaken is to determine how the health care manufacturing sector in Canada can capitalize on domestic growth prospects and maximize its contribution to the Canadian economy through sound industrial development. The study outline has not yet been finalized but it is expected that the study will include, inter alia, the development of a profile of the Canadian industry, a determination of market trends by major product groups, an analysis of the international structure of the industry and how it exerts an influence on Canadian industrial development, an evaluation of the effects of the existing government policy environment on the industry and its development, and an identification of potential research, development and manufacturing opportunities. An in-depth study such as this will require very close cooperation from a number of federal departments, provincial governments and associations representing the private sector's participation in all phases of the study, including its definition, detailed analysis and identification of possible policy options and their impacts will be essential if the desired results are to be obtained.

speechtext:
The only programs whose costs are indexed are: Old Age Security Pensions and the Guaranteed Income Supplement- The payments are indexed quarterly based on the increase in the Consumer Price Index for a previous quarter (i.e. July to September for January; October to December for April; January to March for July; and April to June for October.) Family Allowances-These payments are indexed January each year and are based on the increase in the Consumer Price Index for the 12 month period ending in September of the previous year. War Veterans Allowances-These payments are indexed quarterly using the same formula as the OAS-GIS payments. Was Veterans Disability Pensions-These payments are indexed January each year using the same formula as Family Allowances. Training Allowances under the Occupational Training
Order Paper Questions
Program-These payments are indexed yearly in July using the increase in the average hourly earning in manufacturing for the previous year ending in June. Bill C-19, the Government Expenditure Restraint Act, would eliminate the indexing provision. Unemployment Insurance Benefits-The maximum payments are indexed yearly in January using the increase in the average earnings index. The actual increase in government costs depends on the unemployment experience. speechtext: Yes, the Department of the Environment, Atmospheric Environment Service is the lead agency in Canada with a significant research effort in this area. 1.	Are there regulations currently in effect to control sulfur emissions into the atmosphere (under the Clean Air Act) by oil and coal burning*electric generating plants?
2.	Does the government in any way finance or subsidize the development and installation of flue-gas desulfurization units designed for thermal-electric generating plants?
February 4, 1977

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Fleming (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
1. There are no regulations currently in effect under the Clean Air Act to control emissions of sulphur oxides from oil and coal burning electric generating plants. The Clean Air Act does not give the federal government direct control over emissions of an air pollutant unless it is a significant danger to health. The Department of National Health and Welfare has not, at this time, declared sulphur dioxide to be an air pollutant presenting a significant danger to the health of persons. However, current consideration is being given to a regulation limiting the sulphur content in fuels, under Fuel Provisions of the Clean Air Act. This would have the effect of controlling sulphur emissions from electric generating plants in the same way as direct emission control limit. Also under preparation is a National Emission Guideline for the Thermal Power Generating Industry with stated limits on sulphur dioxide emissions.
2. There is no direct subsidy program for pollution control equipment such as flue gas desulphurization units for thermal-electric power plants. However, the government does have a funding program for the Demonstration of Pollution Abatement Technology (DPAT). This program could be used to cost share under contract with an industry, the demonstration of new flue gas desulphurization technology. These funds, however would normally be restricted to one installation of a type. Under the program, the technology then becomes available for use by all similar plants in Canada. Flue gas desulphurization units would also qualify for the Accelerated Capital Cost Allowance program that allows fast write-off of money spent on pollution control equipment.

speechtext: In so far as the Foreign Investment Review Agency is concerned: Imasco Limited, a subsidiary of British American Tobacco Company, acquired control of Grissol Foods Limited in May 1972. As the provisions of the Foreign Investment Review Act pertaining to the acquisition of control of Canadian business enterprises by non-residents did not come into force until April 9, 1974, and as they did not apply retroactively, the above noted acquisition was not subject to review under the Foreign Investment Review Act.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the agreement of the House to take a look at these amendments, which might not have reached your attention because of the imposition of closure, I should like to bring a matter to the minister's attention in the line of an amendment. We may not reach the section because of closure, but it seems to me to be a very important matter. The minister may have been considering an amendment along this line, in which case I should like to bring the matter to his attention now and find out what his plans are.
What I am referring to is a practice that seems to be a racket which has developed with registered retirement savings plans. A spouse goes to a financial institution and deposits an amount of money, which could be $1,000, $2,000 or, when the bill passes, a larger amount. The spouse for whom the money is deposited has no taxable income. Then the next day the spouse who does have taxable income withdraws the amount of money that was placed in the financial institution, pays a nominal administration fee for having taken out a registered retirement savings plan, which can be with a trust company or other financial institution, and then is able to use it to lessen their income tax liability.
I understand this matter has been brought to the attention of the finance department and is being reviewed. Therefore, I ask the minister whether the matter has been brought to his attention and whether it is possible under the act for someone to behave in this way. If so, does he intend to move an amendment to close this loophole and prevent this kind of rip-off from taking place? If I have not made myself clear, I would be very happy to repeat this procedure which has been brought to my attention.

Mr. Chairman, I can advise the hon. member that the matter is under consideration. I am not sure that the consideration is mature enough that we have an amendment to move at this point, but it is a question we are taking into consideration for the next budget in several months' time.

speechtext: Order. We understand at the table that clauses 24 to 30 were stood. Is that correct?

On clause 24.

Mr. Chairman, may I continue with this matter? I beg your indulgence and the indulgence of the committee in this regard for the same reason we accorded the courtesy to the minister to allow him to place his amendments.
February 4, 1977

I think this is a terribly important matter which needs to be cleared up, and since it relates to amendments generally the committee has been disposed to standing certain things in order to deal with possible amendments before it. I would like to take up this matter until we can get some kind of answer from the minister, because it seems to me that this is an incredible kind of loophole and that people will be able to indulge in an incredible racket if in fact it is so.
It seems that the minister has implied in his statements that in fact some people can work a racket under the income tax law because of the way it is written now. This is what I want to know from the minister. Is it taking place, and, if so, I think the House needs some assurance that this will not be dealt with in the next budget but will be dealt with right now. I raise it today because we still have an hour or so to debate this matter on Monday. Over the weekend the minister and his officials could glance at the appropriate clauses and draft an amendment.
We could stand the debate at a certain point on Monday and have this amendment introduced. Since the House has been disposed to go along with this procedure, we could close this loophole. Aside from the general objections we have been raising to the disproportionate benefits that the wealthy are getting from this bill, to allow them this kind of loophole and to allow them to work this kind of racket compounds the injustice. I think we really need some kind of answer from the minister.

Mr. Chairman, the assessment that I have received of the situation is that if such a procedure is possible-and I gather from conversations with Revenue Canada that they are not totally satisfied that it can be done from a legal standpoint-the possible exposure of the fiscal authorities in this particular situation is quite limited. So there are really two elements to be considered: the first is that some question has been raised as to whether this can be done legally, and the second is the more practical consideration that if it can, how much is involved in terms of the tax laws? On the other hand, the problem which has arisen is to resolve the kind of question the hon. member raised, that is, to find some effective means of dealing with the situation if there is any loophole in that regard. The judgment in this regard has not yet matured, but the feeling is that the risk involved is not substantial.

Mr. Chairman, certainly the minister's answer cannot be acceptable. His argument is that they are not quite sure whether or not it is legal. In fact, people are doing it and are assuming it is legal. They are getting advice to do it, and trust companies are going along with it. Obviously, they have had a look at the legal implications. The fact that relatively few people are doing it and, therefore, because there is not that much of a loss to the treasury, it should be overlooked, seems a pretty shaky argument for the Minister of Finance to make.
As to the remedy, I do not pose as an expert in drafting legislation. Certainly, one of the things that could be done to

close this loophole is to say that these registered retirement savings plans have to be held for a specific period of time in order to avoid this one day in, the next day out, practice to get the benefit. Who is going to do it? It certainly will not be my steelworker who will do it. The guy who will do it is one who can get good tax lawyers and accountants to give him advice on how it can be worked. People in the highest income tax brackets will take advantage of the situation.
Don't kid yourself; it is practised by others, too.

I am glad it is now being confirmed by the hon. member for Edmonton West. I do not really pay too much attention to what the minister's advisers tell me, competent as they are, but when the hon. member for Edmonton West intervenes to tell me that it is so, 1 take it as being so.
Loopholes are not only for the wealthiest taxpayers. If there is one, it is used by others.

If a poor man had $11,000 worth of savings with which he could move through these loopholes, I would accept it. But I do not care whether it is the poor or the rich who use it: it is wrong to have this kind of loophole; and to say it does not cost the treasury a great deal is wrong. This is a racket, and I think it is our obligation to make sure that a loophole that permits this kind of racket is stopped before this bill goes through. I think the minister should give the House some assurance that he will do something about it.

The comment I just made is that I think the hon. gentleman is exaggerating the problem. He says he knows lots of people who are doing it. There are lots of people who may be going ahead and doing other things under the tax law, but they wind up having themselves reassessed. So the fact that someone makes a mistake in his judgment of the tax law may involve him in due course in the payment of more tax. As I have said, the question has been recognized. There has been some discussion as to whether or not the advice which private parties have been taking is well given. The hon. gentleman suggests there would be a massive leak from Revenue Canada in this regard. Certainly that is not the feeling held by my advisers.

I rise on another point of order, Mr. Chairman. I did not suggest for one moment that there is a massive attack on the treasury. I accepted the minister's statement that while this may not constitute a very large loss to the treasury, that was not my point. My point was that it was dishonest and a loophole. Despite the assurance of the minister that it would not cost the treasury very much, it is a bad thing for the government to allow. This was the point I was making. I would like a statement from the minister at least to that extent. He says that they are liable to find themselves in trouble if they take this advice. Is there anything in this legislation which makes illegal the kind of practice I brought to the attention of the minister?

speechtext:
Order, please. When the committee rose at one o'clock, clause 24 was under consideration, and the hon. member for Timmins had the floor.
On clause 24.

Mr. Chairman, after I read clause 24 of Bill C-22 I requested some explanations from the minister's officials with regard to the meaning of the clause and its implications. I wonder if the minister could enlarge on those explanations today so that the matter can be clear in my mind. The officials of the minister's department indicated to me that this clause is to allow all taxpayers to deduct in the year in which they are incurred 100 per cent of their exploration expenses.
In a subsequent paragraph in the letter I received from the officials the only thing that is mentioned with regard to the Canadian development expense account is the acquisition of Canadian resource property. I would like the minister to confirm that both the acquisition of a property and the additional exploration expenses which are added to that acquisition go to what is called the Canadian development expense account in order to establish the value of that property or the cost of that property to the investor.
Second, I would like the minister to confirm that the exploration expenses are treated as an income allowance rather than as a revenue allowance and therefore are not recoverable on the disposal of the property, like depreciation or capital cost allowances. In other words, normally when a piece of equipment or property is sold, the capital cost allowance is recoverable by the government or the tax system. I would like to confirm that this is not so with regard to the exploration expenses which are added to the acquisition of a property.
Finally, at the time of disposal of a property, I would like to know whether the difference between the income from the property and the cost which has been entered in the Canadian development expense account is the profit, and I would like to have the minister confirm whether that profit is considered as a capital gain or as normal income. I hope it would be a capital gain, because I think there is justification for it. If it is normal income, I would like the minister to confirm whether there is

not justification for differentiating between the source of that income, whether it is a normal development corporation, whether the main business of the corporation involved is exploration and development, or what have you. I think there should be a difference if the investment is simply an incidental one, if it involves just a small individual or a small corporation which has invested in the acquisition and development of such a property, and if it is not its normal business and it is just to help in the development of resources in Canada.
The law as it presently stands indicates that if payment for a mineral property, for instance, is made in shares, that is considered a capital gain; but if payment is made in cash, it is considered normal income. I suggest that there is some confusion there. I placed this matter before the former minister. It was my view that the designation of revenues as capital gains or normal income should not be determined by the source or the kind of payment-whether it be shares or cash-but rather by the type of transaction. I put this to the former minister. I should now like to put it to the hon. minister opposite and urge him to consider that the revenue derived from the sale of property should not be determined by whether it is shares or cash but, rather, by the type of transaction.
[DOT] (MIO)

Mr. Chairman, on the first question raised by the hon. member, I can confirm that in our judgment both the acquisition cost of additional exploration and development expenses would be deductible for the purpose of this exemption. On the third question, my understanding is-and this is from the application of the law under the principal business exception-that this in the normal course will be treated as normal income rather than capital gain. On the second question, I just cannot remember offiiand whether there is a recapture upon disposal or not. I am afraid the best I can do is undertake tp make an inquiry and respond further. I cannot give a tax opinion this afternoon, but if the hon. member wants to make a representation on the point I shall be glad to hear it.

Mr. Chairman, if I may, I again make a small plea to the minister with regard to capital gains. If the property registered in the Canadian development expense account is sold, under the present laws the revenue derived therefrom, if paid in shares, would become capital gains, so there is a difference there that presents some confusion. Maybe the minister could look into this matter at the same time and see if the confusion could be cleared up.
I am quite prepared to do so, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I am glad, generally, to see clauses 24, 25 and 26 because they are aiming at removal of the principal occupation rule. It was rather interesting yesterday evening to hear the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie engage in a full-scale attack upon Imperial Oil. As it is a principal occupation business corporation, I suggest the whole exercise of his speech
February 4, 1977

was totally irrelevant and had no application whatsoever to this proposal in the Income Tax Act.
It is rather interesting that we are celebrating this month the thirtieth anniversary of the discovery of LeDuc No. 1 which opened up the Alberta oil development industry. It is unfortunate that at that time and up to now the principal occupation rule had any place in the Income Tax Act. I recall a period of ten years when there was still room for the small-time operators and people who were in the oil development business to acquire freehold leases or overrides on the royalties, that it was always guaranteed that in about 80 per cent of the cases Canadians were outbid by Americans. Lease-hounds and agents of American investors were in on the oil patch like flies around a honey-pot. That was to be expected. After all, there was no expertise in Canada for the development of oil fields. The drillers, equipment dealers and those with any knowledge of developing oil came from the United States in the same way they moved from Canada elsewhere when the oil play was over in the prairies.
One of the difficulties was that, say, a Canadian syndicate wanted to drill a D-2 well which would require $70,000 to $85,000: it could be made up of a couple of farmers, a garage owner, a druggist, a doctor, or whoever wanted to get together in a partnership and put up $10,000 or $15,000. Unfortunately, oil well drilling is a highly speculative business. Three holes out of four holes drilled could be dry. Up to a few years ago the law has consistently been that the recovery of drilling expenses could only be made against the revenue of any producing wells. If there were no producing wells, the money was gone.
Of course, dry wells took up as much money as producing wells. Our American friends, under American law, could offset their lost drilling expenses against ordinary income and therefore recover and recycle into what you might call exploratory working capital the allowances that they could make against ordinary income. Many persons, including myself, tried to convince the Canadian government to do this through ministers of finance and their advisers who unfortunately had a "made in central Canada" bent of mind and did not understand the oil business and rejected these proposals year in and year out.
A few years ago, in a two-step operation, up to 30 per cent was allowed and now the minister proposes to increase that to 100 per cent. I want to congratulate the minister and his officials on this. Maybe the fact that there is now a deputy minister who worked a long time in Saskatchewan helped in this regard. In any case, I commend the government even though it is pretty well locking the stable door after all but the last horse has been stolen.
I should now like to hear from the minister whether clauses 24 and 25 will effectively allow an individual or corporation who is not in the petroleum development business to write off 100 per cent of its contributions to exploration and development against income other than that arising out of the production of oil and gas. Or is there some residual formula which would phase it out over a number of years?
Income Tax

Mr. Chairman, the amendment is only applicable for a trial period. That is, it will apply to investments made during the trial period. Otherwise, a taxpayer in that situation will be treated in exactly the same way as a principal business taxpayer in the sense that he can apply this expenditure entirely to income.
Mr. Chairman, am I correct in assuming that the trial period is to run for three years?
Mr. Chairman, yes, up to July, 1979. It started last May.

May I ask another question about the trial period, Mr. Chairman? Does the minister envisage a continuing review, because once we reach the last year of the trial period there could be great uncertainty as to whether it will be continued, and that uncertainty, quite naturally, would inhibit future development plans?

Mr. Chairman, I recognize that. The trial period has been instituted really for the purpose of seeing how effective we shall be in attracting exploration. We are having some early success and there is some indication already that funds are being used in this way. We shall want to overcome the potential hiatus which could occur as we approach the anniversary date.
Thank you, sir.

Mr. Chairman, the present measure is an about-face on the part of the government. Over the years, at least ever since I have been a member of this House, the government has been most reluctant to make available to the oil, gas and mining industries the benefit of the principal income clause. I remember many years ago being asked to invest in an oil well. At that time I did not have any money, but two or three years later I asked if I could invest because I was interested in an investment which I considered about as safe as a horse race. The person who had earlier asked me to invest had drilled some oil wells himself. He said that there was no money in oil, that the government had enacted a certain law with regard to principal income, and there was not much point in investing in an Alberta oil well. Actually, I was interested in an oil well in the Lloydminster field. A few years ago the then minister of finance-Mr. Benson I think- amended the tax act and allowed deductions of up to 30 per cent. At least that was a good start. But you had to wait for about five years before you got your money back if you invested in certain resource industries.
Without doubt, the existence of the particular section of the act we are now discussing is largely responsible for the predominant American ownership of the oil industry in western Canada. Unless that law is changed, the outlook for oil and gas drilling in this country will not be good. At least it will not be easy for individuals to become part owners of oil wells. Unfortunately, Canadian oil, gas and mining industries are not doing as well as they should. I understand that for the first

February 4, 1977
Income Tax
time in many years, this year no new mine has been opened in Ontario. In northern Manitoba a good many mines have closed or are closing, and activity is at a low level. I understand that only one diamond drilling outfit is operating in northern Manitoba, whereas normally you would see between 30 and 40 operating there. Companies in this field seem to have moved their operations across the border. One cannot blame the federal government entirely for this, although to some extent the controversy between the provincial and federal governments has led to the slowdown in investment in our oil, gas and mining industries.
We have often been told that we must spend a great deal of money if we are to be self-reliant in energy. One hears talk of self-reliance in the mining field by 1985 or some time in the future. I shall make two or three points and then sit down. I was much taken by something the Canada West Foundation in Calgary said recently. It had some things to say about the implementation of guidelines for national resource policies which should be established for the country's long-term interest. For example, it was proposed that the general structure and basic level of taxes imposed on the non-renewable resource sector should be reassessed by provincial and federal governments acting together. It was also proposed that a single definition of resource income directly related to ability to pay and mutually acceptable to federal and provincial governments should serve as a basis for all income-related taxes.
Mr. Chairman, federal and provincial people are still not sitting down with a clearcut policy in mind. They are still confronting one another, and confrontation is hardly in the national interest. Although certain amendments to the tax act are welcome, I suggest that until the federal and provincial governments decide on a single, reasonable, uniform taxation policy with regard to our resources, we shall not advance much.

Mr. Chairman, I listened to the hon. member for Edmonton West and was struck by how we can look at the same set of facts and come to different conclusions about them. The act we are discussing has been in existence for a long time. I suspect that it would not be quite the same as it now is if the hon. member for Edmonton West and I had not served in this House at the same time.
I want to talk about the oil industry and raise some questions. The government is introducing measures similar to those which were discredited in the past. Essentially, the government's measures are designed to encourage, by the provision of depletion allowances and write-offs of various kinds, excessive exploration and overinvestment in the oil industry. We are going to wind up being back in our old position, although under somewhat different circumstances.
The hon. member for Edmonton West drew on his profound experience and knowledge of the oil industry and said that the United States has offered many advantages to its investors which our country has not offered our investors. That is only half the story. At one time we offered as many advantages to investors within the industry as the United States has been offering.
Not at all.

The truth is that the advantages the United States has offered its investors has been an ongoing scandal in that country and members of Congress and the United States Senate have continually risen to denounce the concessions made over the years to the oil industry.
Let us consider what has happened to the oil industry in Canada. What has been the result of concessions which the Alberta government and other governments have given to the oil industry in order to encourage it to look for oil? The conclusion we must come to from an examination of the figures is that we so stimulated the oil industry to produce that we had oil coming out of our ears. We literally gave it away because we could not do anything else with it. We had to give it away. Then, when we needed the oil, we did not have it.
Let us consider how we have encouraged exploration in Canada. What has been the history of exploration? We encouraged exploration and drilling so much, particularly in Alberta, that we produced a glut of oil. We could not use for ourselves all our own oil coming out of our wells; ultimately, we prorated the production of those wells. Wells were forced to operate at between 30 per cent and 35 per cent of capacity because we could not use all our own oil. There was no market for it. What did we do? We said we must export our oil. We pleaded with the United States to take it. Our National Energy Board, acting under our national oil policy, allowed us to sell oil to the United States at between $1.50 and $2 per barrel. Nobody had any conception that this is a finite resource, that there is just so much oil in the ground and when it is gone it is gone. We did that for about ten years, only to discover to our horror that all the information on proven and potential resources that had been given to us by the oil companies was just a pack of lies. It was not true. We found ourselves in a crisis.
When the OPEC countries decided to raise their price and put the squeeze on Canada, we were vulnerable. That is what stimulation through taxation in the oil industry did for us. It left us exposed. It encouraged an overproduction of a commodity that would have been better left in the ground until needed in the future. We need it today and we will need it in the future.
I see the same situation with regard to this method. There is no future. We cannot solve future energy problems by pulling the oil out as rapidly as possible. As a matter of fact, it would probably be most useful if we left the oil in the ground and used it for petrochemicals in the future, rather than burning it now in our furnaces and refineries.
We are kidding ourselves. How long will the oil last? Supposing we do find some-how much will it be? We have already taken most of it out of the ground. It is very difficult to find, and what we do find is in small amounts. However, we go ahead with the same kind of pattern that created disaster for us in the past and will lead to disaster in the future. When
February 4, 1977

the time comes when it will be needed for the petrochemical industry in Alberta, it will not be there. Alberta is doing very well today. I am pleased that it is doing well. However, the people of Alberta know they are dealing with a finite resource. They know they have to husband that resource in a particular way in order to have a prolonged and ongoing industry, particularly in petrochemicals.
What do we do? We tell the oil companies to go there, find the oil, use it and get rid of it as quickly as they can. What shortsightedness; what foolishness! Rather than encouraging the finding and production of this resource, we should be discouraging it in order to save it for the future. Future generations will look upon us as having been the most stupid people on the face of the earth because of what we are doing with our resources. It took billions and billions of years for that small amount of oil to be produced and settle itself in pools in the ground. We have taken only one generation, two at the most, to deplete that resource of billions of years, leaving virtually nothing for future generations. It is tax measures of this kind which have assisted this despoiling of our resources.
Going back to the situation in Alberta, I ask the hon. member for Edmonton West whether, in retrospect, it would not have been better to provide less encouragement to production in those early years. The production was going to take place anyway. Suppose we had not produced that oil as quickly as we did. We would not have had to export it. We would not have had to look for markets outside our own country. We would have had a supply of oil for the future infinitely greater and more valuable today, instead of giving it away for what we did. It was a foolish policy.
How did the hon. member for Edmonton West view that kind of approach? I am sure there are many people in his province of Alberta who see the folly of that kind of policy. I am sure they would have preferred a gradual development based on Canada's needs, rather than based on investors pulling out as much as they could in order to make a fast buck. I see the hon. member for Edmonton West shakes his head. After that lesson, has he not learned anything about the use of resources? I see he wants to rise and reply. I am quite prepared to yield the floor to the hon. member for Edmonton West, if he wishes.

Mr. Chairman, I will make a short comment. This is not a debate on oil development policy. As a quick observation, I will say that hindsight sometimes is a very cheap commodity and the conclusions based upon it are just as valuable.

I agree that it is very easy to have hindsight and to come to some conclusion about hindsight. The point 1 am trying to make to the hon. member for Edmonton West and, hopefully, to the hon. minister is, let us not repeat the same mistake. In those days, the same sense of urgency arose and the same speeches were made. We had to bonus the investor to explore and produce oil, thinking that today was the only framework in which we were to operate, that there was not going to be a tomorrow. That is the point I am trying
Income Tax
to make. Let us not repeat the same stupid error we committed in the oil industry in the past.
This is a bad piece of legislation, one that I personally am not prepared to vote for. What would we accomplish doing this? We would probably make some people very rich. We would allow them to shelter a lot of their tax through exploration. I could perhaps even go along with that, if it were the only way of doing it. I do not say that I would like it, but if there was a compelling need, we had to have the oil immediately, and something would happen if we did not, and that the oil today would be more important now than in the future, we would have to cut some corners. If we had to drop some equity in our tax system to accomplish that, I could understand it. I may not like it, but I could understand it.
However, when we drop equity and provide an enormous bonus to the wealthy of Canada to find a tax shelter through exploration, damaging the country at the same time by their activities, that is an outstanding example of insanity. Let me read to the committee what has been said about this situation. I quote from the Financial Times of November 8, 1976. The article talks about units sold by Midland Doherty Limited acting as agent for Ranchmens:
Minimum subscription is $10,000 with increments of $5,000. The issue and its pricing is deliberately designed to appeal to investors in 50 per cent and up tax brackets.
That is who it is designed for. I am sure the hon. member for Edmonton West will not repeat his speech of the other day and say that this is something for the little man. It is obvious that those who stand to benefit most from this kind of investment are those who have tax liabilities and cannot find loopholes. Therefore, the government has opened up a new one for them. They can invest in the oil exploration industry and write off the total cost of their investment in oil exploration and production against their tax liability. Later they will come back here to us or other legislators who may be around and use what they got for nothing from tax money as a cost basis for determining what they should get for oil. In other words, the oil companies will do as they are doing now. They will say they need more money because it costs so much to produce oil. They will not say that what they are claiming as costs were in fact depreciation and depletion allowances which were bonuses from the various levels of government. They do not pay for them. It is money saved in the tax system.
At some point I should like to ask the minister whether these benefits which are being given to investors in the oil industry will some day form a cost basis for them, whether that will be recognized as a cost basis despite the fact that the money really came through a savings in the tax system-not all the money, but a substantial part of it: for instance, if taxpayers are in the 50 per cent tax bracket and they invest $100 in the oil industry, then they have invested $50 and the government has invested $50 and it is an investment on the part of the government, because it is not as though the government had no alternative, the government could collect the tax from people in the 50 per cent bracket and divert it to

February 4, 1977
Income Tax
Petro-Can. We can do our own financing. We can do our own exploration. After all, 1 presume that was what Petro-Can was set up for. Petro-Can is capable of doing it. If it is not capable of doing so, it can certainly be the entrepreneur. It can hire drillers in the same way as somebody in Texas can hire drillers, or somebody from Bay Street, Toronto.
So it is really being done with our money, and later on they will not come back and say the cost basis upon which we think the oil should be priced is 50-cent dollars. They will say it is $1 dollars and they will want a return on that amount even though half the risk and half the investment came from the people of Canada.
The point to make about depriving the federal treasury of revenue at this level is that there is no such thing as income tax avoidance. The extent to which one group of people does not pay the tax it should means that another group of Canadians has to make up for it. So the oil investment bonanza becomes a burden to the small taxpayers.
Hon. members in the Conservative party will say," It doesn't have to be that way; we can reduce government expenditures instead." Well, of course, we could reduce old age pensions and family allowances and achieve the same result, but I am sure that is not what we want to do, and that is not going to happen because the people are not going to let it happen. But this kind of thing does happen because it is not highly visible, it is not obvious; it gets buried in the tax system, this great subsidy to the rich of Canada, and the subsidy which is paid to them has to be made up by the smaller taxpayers.
Let me continue by quoting from an article by Jack McArthur which appeared in the Toronto Star of December 16, 1976:
When you fear for Canada's future and wish you had less money tied up in Quebec ... when profits have gone flat in the manufacturing of cigarettes, booze, beer and a dozen other products... when big Government and its confusing controls seem to make life hardly worth living . .. when those worries are jabbing at the old ulcer, you go looking for oil and natural gas in Western Canada.
This article was written with reference to the amendment before us now. The writer concludes by saying:
Some of the enthusiasm in Canada stems from last May's federal budget.
Finance minister Donald Macdonald had a carrot for those whose main businesses are not in natural resources. For three years, they would be able to write off immediately for tax purposes the costs of looking for resources. This deduction reduces taxes on their other activities. Ottawa's idea was clear. It wanted more money looking for oil and gas and was prepared to give tax-breaks to get it.
With so many reasons for investing in exploration and production, it's no wonder the Toronto Stock Exchange index of prices of western oil shares has jumped almost 10 per cent since mid-November.
I don't know what it would take to arouse this committee, to make it see that we are repeating a mistake of the past by providing tax benefits of this kind in connection with exploration for oil. If there were a possibility that exploration for oil would enable us to meet the projected energy needs of the future for any substantial period in the future, it could be understood, but all we are looking at is, at best, a short period of relief. The real solution for the future is conservation, as the minister himself pointed out when he was minister of energy,

mines and resources. The logic he displayed as minister of energy, mines and resources is being confounded by what he is doing today as Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?

I should like to put to the minister the questions to which I alluded in my remarks. Would he give us an explanation of the clause which states that the various benefits received from governments, forgivable loans, deductions from royalties, investment allowance, and so on, will not reduce the amount people will be able to deduct under this clause? That is how I read it; they can receive all those other benefits without having this kind of allowance reduced.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, in the situation in which a provincial government has taken steps to provide that kind of incentive, it would seem to be perverse to treat it adversely from a federal taxation standpoint.

So this particular arrangement, if a person is in the 50 per cent tax bracket, means that 50 per cent of the money he is investing comes from the federal government, and if provincial governments allow them another set of money it is theoretically possible that if a person plays very cagily and gets different concessions he could be working almost totally with government money in terms of the development of this industry. I see the minister does not want to deal with that aspect as a theoretical proposition.

One way or other, the fellow will incur expenses. Since he is not paying a 100 per cent tax rate it is not clear to me how he can get all those expenses back. It certainly will reduce his tax liability, but I do not quite follow the mathematics.

Well, you are providing him basically with free capital, 50 per cent under this provision. If he is in the 50 per cent tax bracket, for every $ 100 he invests he only puts up $50 of his own money; the extra $50 is money he has saved in terms of his tax liability. In other words, his own capital is only half of what it would otherwise be for investment purposes. What would be his cost base later on? Let us suppose the AIB continues. Will it be the money he put in? I do not see how it can be. So will it be the total amount put in?
His cost base will be his expenditure, but for ultimate purposes the amount of his expenses will be deducted.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct the minister's attention to what has happened in northern Manitoba as far as exploration goes. At the present time, mining is our main industry but there is literally no exploration going on in northern Manitoba. I can remember a time when there were up to 28 diamond drilling rigs engaged in exploration work in the north. It seems to me that as the federal government and provincial governments try to get more and more tax dollars out of the industry, the industry becomes increasingly less inclined to undertake the risk of
February 4, 1977

engaging in exploration work. They question whether it will bring sufficient return to their investors or shareholders.
The province of Manitoba is paying 50 per cent of the cost of exploration. However, it does not have many takers at this time, for the simple reason that the industry, knowing very well how governments operate, realizes that there is going to be nothing left for the industry if any finds are made. In the province of Manitoba $1 million has been spent on exploration so far, and 1 do not think that even the crews have gone out into the bush to this point. So I think we have to be very careful, if we do want to encourage development, that we do not tax industry to death before it ever gets started.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said when he went to the United States last week that our future is in the untapped resources of the north. Unless government is prepared to take the same kind of risk that industry takes in the field of exploration, then the government had better take over all the exploration work in the area. This is what the province is trying to do and it is just not working out.
Industry itself is not expanding in the north but is simply mining what it has found to date. Exploration is moth-balled for the time being until there is some realization that it is a costly business to explore, to diamond drill, and so on, in the north where costs are prohibitive. The government does not seem to take these things into consideration. The cost of exploration has skyrocketed. Companies like International Nickel have moved their exploration crews completely out of the north and are operating out of Ontario at the present time. A company like Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting has absolutely curtailed all exploration in northern Manitoba and the north in general, for the simple reason that they cannot show a decent return to their shareholders in view of the tax that is required by the federal and provincial governments. Sherrit Gordon at the present time are closing down parts of their operation; they are also faced with the same situation, with no exploration work going on whatsoever.
So far as this bill is concerned, we should be thinking very seriously of encouraging industry to go into the north. To do this we have also to provide incentive through having a less firm hand on the tax side of it in order to encourage development. I am not for giving everything away, Mr. Chairman, but I still think that private industry can do a far better job of exploration than the government.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask one question of the minister. It is some time now since the budget; I think I understood it on budget night and I did look into it. Is the clause of the bill that we are dealing with now the one dealing with the encouragement of exploration and development? Is it the clause that provides for individuals and corporations taking so much money off their taxable income provided that, within a certain period of time, they invest the money in exploration and development?
Income Tax

Yes, Mr. Chairman. It is dealing specifically with individuals and corporations whose principal business is not resource exploration and development. As the hon. member will recall, somebody whose principal business was of this character previously had that advantage, and we have now extended it to others in the community.

Then may I just say a few words on that for a moment. I want to congratulate the government on this clause. I hope that members in all parties in the House, including the socialists, might appreciate that we are now reaching the stage where probably the greatest problem we have to face, not only on this continent but throughout the world, is the cost of energy. The cost of energy is one of the main factors creating inflation. If there is sufficient exploration and development to make sure that we are self-sufficient in this country in gas and oil, then we have gone a long way; and the government has gone a long way if it offers encouragement of this sort in order to control inflation other than by way of wage and price controls.
As I have said before, when we are dealing with this subject there is one thing that is always overlooked. I see the hon. member for Calgary South here; he has had a lot of experience in this field. When you are looking for investment for exploration and development purposes in the gas and oil field, you are not competing in Canada, you are competing throughout the world. Unless we give the industry incentives and let the industry benefit under this provision, then drilling equipment and other items of equipment will be sent to the North Sea and elsewhere in the world. We will be the losers. We will be paying $12, $13, $15 or $20 a barrel for crude petroleum if we do not develop our own supplies.
I hope this is a matter to which hon. members will direct their attention. I agree with the last speaker that, whatever the industry, there is ample evidence that private enterprise, particularly when risk capital is involved, certainly in my opinion can do a much better job than state control. Even communist countries are making deals with free enterprise and entrepreneurs in the United States and Canada to drill for gas and oil, because they realize that communist countries have complete state control and that there will be greater efficiency with free enterprise or in partnership with free enterprise. Surely that is ample evidence of the direction in which this country should be going, rather than in a socialist direction. If the United Kingdom's reserves are proven, as now appears is the case in the North Sea, then they may be able to pull themselves out of the economic collapse they have suffered during the last few years. I do not want to repeat what I said last evening about where some of the blame might lie.
This is one clause of the bill to which I think the government and the minister's department have given a lot of thought. I want to congratulate the government on being realistic enough to realize that exploration and development of gas and oil today must continue at an accelerated pace; otherwise we will no longer be self-sufficient in this field.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the hon. member would permit me to direct a number of questions to him with regard to some of the remarks he has just made?

speechtext: Let us get on with the bill.
This has to do directly with the bill.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: All kinds of people are waiting for a refund. Let us get on with the bill.

It is directly on this particular clause. The hon. member for Calgary North was talking about free enterprise in the oil industry. In fact, Mr. Chairman, the oil industry is hardly free enterprise any more in terms of who gets the benefits. Let me ask the hon. member for Calgary North, who is very knowledgeable about these things, this question. Of the present price of a barrel of oil, how much goes to the oil industry, how much to the federal government and how much to the government of Alberta? The reason I ask this question is pretty obvious: I think something like 60 per cent to 70 per cent of the price of a barrel of oil does not go to private enterprise at all; it goes to public enterprise, the government of Alberta.

Well, my hon. friend has already answered the question. I like to be helped, and when a member asks me a question I like to help him. Now the hon. member has given me the answer. What he is trying to say, Mr. Chairman, is that the industry is sort of split between government enterprise and private enterprise. But I think he has missed the point, and I will clear it up for him quickly. Certainly, the greater share of the revenue today is going to government, and this will discourage exploration and development in the oil and gas field. This is what the government is trying to relieve.
The point I am making is that when you invest risk capital you should do it efficiently. To put a hole in the ground, drill it and organize the whole operation technically, is done more efficiently under the free enterprise system than by the government. It is true that these corporations and individuals pay large taxes. That has been the great complaint. I think my good friend, perhaps unintentionally because I know what his business was before he came to the House, missed the point.

I will make another point, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member for Calgary North has an argument for supporting the government very strongly on this measure. He said that this is one way of significantly lowering the price of energy in Canada.
I did not say that at all.

It seems to me that the province he comes from is taking the position that when the OPEC countries raise the price of energy by 400 per cent, as they did a few years ago, the province of Alberta is entitled to the same amount, and the reason it has not done so is because of the confrontation between the federal and provincial governments on this

matter, with the province of Alberta kicking and screaming about not being allowed to raise its price. Therefore I would like to ask the hon. member for Calgary North how the price of energy can be lowered if it is the policy of the oil producing provinces to raise it to world levels.

I will answer that question, Mr. Chairman, but I am not the Minister of Finance as yet. It is his job to answer these questions. But let me say this to him. He talks in his preamble about Alberta. The reason there is no development or exploration going on in Saskatchewan is that whatever Alberta might have done, they pay twice as much in taxes. You only have to talk to the top men in Calgary and they will tell you that it really costs them money now to produce a barrel of crude petroleum in Saskatchewan, so they pump it so slowly that none will come out. If that is the kind of development under a socialist government which my friend likes, it is not the kind I would accept.
Certainly if we explore and develop resources and find certain quantities of oil, perhaps cheaper energy will be provided. I know that if my friend were minister of finance, like his governments in Saskatchewan and Manitoba which have their two hands in the till all the time, the price of oil would not go down. But the way to lower the price of energy-and I say this to him in terms of sound economics-is to cut down taxes, not increase them. His philosophy is to increase them and to discourage exploration and development.
I do not mind answering his questions, but I realize there is a time limit on this debate. I am not really wasting any time because finally their filibuster will have to end.
