speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I wonder if I should allow this exchange between hon. members to continue. The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge asked questions of another hon. member, not of the minister, then yielded the floor, regardless of whether the Chairman agreed or not, and regardless of another hon. member who might be interested in seeking the floor. To allow the committee time to reach a decision and to re-examine this procedure, I call upon the hon. member for Calgary South.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister a question. Do I understand correctly that on development expenses rather than exploration expenses the write-off is 30 per cent a year on a diminishing balance?
Yes, that is right, Mr. Chairman.

I would like to ask the minister how he arrived at this in view of the fact that exploration is a key factor in finding additional reserves. One of the great problems we will face in this country is the development of reserves and production in the high cost frontier areas. I recall reading recently that a fully developed production platform in the North Sea will cost in the order of $1 billion.
February 4, 1977

One of the problems we are facing in this country is not only Finding the reserves but justifying the investment to put these reserves on production, thus making them viable. Has the minister given any thought to making development expenses fully deductible in view of the fact that this would be an important factor in making certain that off-shore fields which would be uneconomical today would become economical to develop? Perhaps Sable Island or the area surrounding it is a good example of a very high cost area. I recall, for instance, the construction of a pipeline there costing in excess of $1 million a mile. I wonder therefore if the minister is prepared to reconsider making development expenses fully deductible, thus making off-shore reserves an economical production.

Mr. Chairman, the real purpose was to provide an incentive at the highest risk end of the operation, namely, the exploration cost which would be involved potentially, such as if you are going to drill two or three holes and might Find nothing but dry holes. Naturally when you move to the development phase, you have assessed for yourself that there are good chances of finding something. At that point the development can be more easily financed than can the highly speculative effect of capital involved in exploration. I do not take issue with the point the hon. member makes about the cost of development. I know it is high, and will be particularly high in the frontier areas. The thought we had in mind in this change was to encourage risk money to explore for additional oil and gas.

Mr. Chairman, I was hoping to direct my question to the hon. member for Calgary North, but I will have to put it to the Minister of Finance. Can the minister tell me what study has been carried out on the effect of this concession with regard to what sort of reserves or potential reserves we might get by increasing the benefits to investors in this Field? Surely when the Department of Finance allows people to do this instead of paying the federal treasury in taxes, they have some idea of the benefits to be derived. How many more years' reserve can we expect to have, and how much more secure will our future be as a result of the concessions the minister is offering to investors in the oil industry?

In this regard you can only talk about the potential of the hydrocarbon bearing zone in Canada. This is a measure of judgment by experts in the field, founded among other things on the drilling experience or, in some cases, the seismic information. On the basis of this and other experience in comparable areas in Canada one can make an estimate of the potential production that can be gained from a particular area. What you cannot estimate is at what time exploration will be successful in tapping that potential, as a succession of Firms have found out. Shell Canada in the late 1930's and 1940's, having the drilling rights to the Leduc field, found it very hard to develop the field there and gave it up to another company, only to suffer the chagrin of seeing another company bring in a wild-cat at that point. Even with all the
Income Tax
scientific assistance one can have, ultimately there is a very high measure of chance involved in putting a drill down.
In response to how many drill holes will be successful as a result of this kind of tax arrangement in the next three years, I cannot really give a speciFic figure. I could seek from my colleague the current estimates of the geological survey of Canada as to the hydro carbon potential of the various areas of Canada, but one can draw the general conclusion that on the whole the more drill holes which are put down, the better chance there is of Finding the resource.
I do not know anyone at this point who can say with any precision how successful we are going to be in a short period of time in bringing on additional oil and natural gas. Certainly we can expect to bring some on, but how much can be expected has to be a matter of chance as much as anything. Unless we take that chance and drill the holes, however, we are definitely not going to get it.

That is the same as playing Russian roulette with taxpayers' money. The reason I asked that question was really to elicit the response I got from the minister. The point is he does not know; nobody knows. We could in fact be pouring this money down the sink hole. We may just be spending this money to Find out how much oil we do not have because, even under the most optimistic examination of our future for hydro carbons, we do not have very much.
How do you know?

Well, that is what they say, and to make a comparison, at Leduc in the early days of oil exploration people did not know very much about it. Scientific ways of discovering oil really had not been worked out very carefully, but today a great deal of work is being done in this country in terms of Finding out what the potential is. We can always strike it lucky on some field, but from everything I have read there do not seem to be any Leducs around any more waiting to be discovered.
At the very best there are small pockets around which may be found; therefore, to provide this kind of stimulus in this game of Russian roulette does not seem to be a terribly wise proposal to put before this committee.

In the first place I take exception to that kind of reasoning. Let us divide the potential up into the more conventional hydro carbon provinces which we have in the western Canada sedimentary basin and then talk about the frontier. It is known and it is clear that there has been some success during the course of the current year, and that there are additional deposits, particularly of natural gas, which can be identified by drilling and brought into the system, so there is something very substantial to be gained with regard to our natural gas supply by additional drilling of this kind.
However, what is even more significant is the fact that seismic indications in the high Arctic and in the Arctic off-

February 4, 1977
Income Tax
shore show that there are very major structures which could be even larger than Leduc in terms of production if these structures are filled with hydro carbons, and I go back to my point: we are not going to identify whether we have a supply of oil and gas unless we drill holes, and we are going to have difficulty raising the funds to drill holes without the kinds of incentives we have right here.
In a perverse way it is even desirable to know that the hydro carbon provinces, for whatever reasons, over geological time may no longer contain hydro carbons. In an economy very substantially based on oil and natural gas, if indeed we do not have any more potential, we should be working very hard at developing alternative sources. If we do have natural gas and oil, I think it is important for the decision making level to find this out as soon as possible by drilling.

On that last statement of the minister I find that I can agree with him completely, and that is one of the things I am getting at. We do in fact know a fair amount now. We do not know as much as we would like to know or should know, but I think it is pretty obvious that we cannot predicate the future on hydro carbons, gas and oil. We must move to other forms of energy.
While I do not have before me the speeches the minister made when he was minister of energy, mines and resources, it seems to me that he said very much the same thing, that if we are to be spending money we should be spending money on new forms of energy instead of just wasting our time and providing tax benefits in a field which is not really very good for the future, even at the most optimistic estimates. Even if more oil and gas were found than expected, how much oil and gas could be found in terms of future supplies? Will there be enough for 25 years or 50 years?
Then we go through the same thing again. The point is that we have to move to new forms of energy, and these things can be marginal until we do find them-they can hold us until we get there-but we should not be placing a heavy reliance on this kind of energy for the future.

I would be glad to deal with that as well. We have in my lifetime found an additional new source of energy in the form of the nuclear power reactor. It has taken very nearly 25 years to move from the theoretical technology involved to the effective commercial exploitation of it. There is a common practice on the part of some observers of energy policy to talk about solar energy, biomass, wind or tidal energy, and to assume that to think about it is to install it with the present technology. However, that has not been our experience in technology. We in this country are going to be dependent-as indeed the world is going to be dependent-on fossil fuel sources, probably for the balance of my lifetime, and I think it is therefore important for Canadians to identify our sources if we can, rather than pay somebody else for them.
In due course I think we are going to evolve effective alternative sources of energy, and that is desirable, but I do not think it is adequate to say that we will stay cold for 20

years and that by then we should have some effective solar technology to take care of us.

Mr. Chairman, further to the question I asked the minister about the 30 per cent diminishing balance writeoff on development expenditures, I am wondering if the minister is aware that any sophisticated company which looks at its exploration program in any off-shore and high risk area at the same time has to run through the economics of producing, before it even gets involved in the early exploration. Does he realize that they examine on a very careful basis whether the land regulations and the tax rules which are in place permit them to develop if there is a discovery of a certain size?
I believe this is an alteration to the rules as they were in the past. In other words, development expenditures were fully deductible, and I suggest to the minister that this is a retrograde step which would make it less attractive to develop. It would discourage explorers from going in in the first place because they recognize the probabilities. They recognize that they have certain chances, but if they fall somewhat short of the reserves they hope to find, then under certain tax rules they could not proceed to develop. I suggest to the minister that this is a discouragement to exploration in the first place. I think this has been evidenced in the North Sea where a great many small companies, particularly Canadian companies, were forced to sell out to bigger companies, simply because they were unable to raise the very large amounts of capital required. I think the minister recognizes that if there is a problem in the energy producing industries of our country today, it is the availability of capital not only for exploration but also for development.
Everybody is short of capital. In fact even the very large companies are, as evidenced by their activities in the recent past. They simply cannot find the sources of capital which are going to be required.
I would like to ask the minister whether he would give consideration to changing this write-off provision and increasing it to 100 per cent, in view of the fact that this government has for a number of years been stingy with regard to everything it has done. It has always been treading the narrow line of being too tough. The minister is well aware of the cutbacks in exploration which have taken place. That is one of the reasons why we have a serious energy outlook in this country at the present time.
I am wondering whether the minister is going to err on the side of being too tough, bearing in mind particularly that there are no rules in place today relating to off-shore areas. We have so many uncertainties, so many unknowns, and so many rules that we err on the side of being too stingy and we have created a very great uncertainty, particularly as it relates to the frontier areas under the control of the government.
I wonder if the minister would consider this question of the 30 per cent write-off for development, recognizing that it would give further stimulus to exploration and would bring less
February 4, 1977

economic fields into the realm of economic fields. Presumably in the slightly longer term it would improve the energy outlook in Canada. It would at least nail down one area as a certainty rather than the basically negative things that have prevailed in recent years, notwithstanding the fact that the basic thrust of this clause, which permits Canadians to invest in exploration, is a good one.

The difficulty, of course, is just how much of the public purse you are going to make available for any of these operations. One could say in a single minded way that you should make all conceivable funds available for this purpose. We have said that as a matter of priority in terms of forming a Canadian energy policy it is important to identify the potential of an area, which is to be done primarily by exploratory drilling. It may well be because of the high capital costs involved in development we would want to look again at the rate of write off for those who at the moment do the exploration drilling we are most concerned to stimulate.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge.

I see the chairman is becoming somewhat familiar with the name of my constituency.
I should like to direct this question to the minister. It will be quite obvious why I am asking, but before I do I wish the minister would not drag out his red herrings about how we are going to be freezing in the dark unless we pass this kind of legislation. There is energy available. There are other forms of energy that can be purchased at this particular time. I want to ask the minister to make a comparison between the kind of tax benefit and loss to the treasury that is going to take place through this measure as against what Canada is spending in trying to develop new forms of energy.
The reason I ask this question is quite obvious. In other words, what is this measure going to cost? How much are we spending in exploring for or examining new forms of energy?

On the second part of the question, Mr. Chairman, I would have to inquire of my colleague as to the expenditure in the private and public area on new forms of energy. On the first part of the question, there is going to be some cost certainly, but it will depend on the extent to which it is seen as an attractive investment by many people. In other words, one of the reasons for having a trial period is so that the government's liability in this area may be limited for the purpose of determining the efficacy of these means of stimulating investment or whether, on the other hand, we may be giving too much away at this point.
I cannot give a precise figure now but I can say that since the matter has come up there have been a number of funds put together for the purpose of engaging in this kind of exploration.

May I first of all say that in principle I am very pleased to see that the question of assistance to dependent children or other persons confined to wheelchairs is being provided. I think this is something long overdue. All of us have personal experience of people who have children who require very close attention, and we are familiar with the costs associated with that care. I am therefore happy to see this particular measure included in the bill. My happiness is somewhat soured-
Tempered.

-tempered, by knowing that I have to say the same thing on this as I have said on some of the other reasonably good measures which are put into the tax bill and then distorted because of the disproportionate benefits they give to the rich as against what they give to people on working incomes.
It must be obvious that the cost of looking after a child in a wheelchair bears as heavily on the poor as it does on the rich; in fact, perhaps more heavily on the poor than on the rich.

February 4, 1977
Income Tax
This allowance is really not going to cover totally the cost of supporting a child of that kind, yet if we look at the effect that this has we can see quite clearly that the better off are going to benefit more from the dependent child disability deduction. Someone with an income of $10,000 a year receives a benefit of $275; someone fortunate enough to have an income of $50,000 a year receives a tax benefit of $563. The higher income receives more than twice as much, and of course it is proportional all the way through.
It seems to me that to distort a humanitarian measure like this is the wrong way of going about things, and I have to object to it. I do not think anything points more significantly to the kinds of things that happen in our society, the kinds of distortions that take place, and the positions in which members of this House are often placed. The government brings in a measure which is humanitarian on the surface and has the support of all people, then deliberately distorts it to maintain the bias between rich and poor in which the rich do better and the poor do worse. The government says, "The poor will get something, so why should they complain if the rich get twice as much? If the poor complain and this bill does not pass, they will get nothing at all."
We should get our handkerchiefs out.

It is easy for my friends on my right to jeer, but let them stand up and tell me on what sense of morality is a measure like this based, a measure designed to assist crippled or disabled children but under which the rich are to be compensated twice as much as the poor. What is worse, if you do not earn any taxable income, you will get nothing. If you are very poor, you get nothing at all. What is the moral basis of this measure?
If you have no taxable income, you do not pay any tax.
Because you do not pay tax, your crippled child will not get benefits.
But there are other programs, you know.

What benefit do you get if you do not pay tax? Mr. Chairman, we are not speaking of a kind of universal demogrant. We are speaking about a deduction from taxable income. If you do not earn taxable income you do not get any benefit. Perhaps we should leave that point. After all, judging from the comments one hears, some hon. members feel that the poor are not deserving and perhaps should not get any benefit.
Let us assume that you earn less income than some other people. Why should you get only half as much of a benefit to assist your disabled child?
Why do you pay more than twice as much tax if you make twice as much money?

I know that this whole business is very symmetrical. Hon. members will repeat the argument of the Minister of Finance, that the tax system is proportionately based and since we are talking about tax reduction, why, this is the way it works. Mr. Chairman, that is a lovely piece of symmetry. But what kind of morality is it? That is what I am asking the committee.
The benefit need not be given in the form of a tax deduction. It could be given as a tax credit. If it were instituted as a tax credit, each person would benefit equally, including the person who does not earn taxable income. That, it seems to me, is the way it ought to be done. It should not be instituted in the form of a tax deduction, because under the present system the more you earn, the greater is the benefit you can obtain.
We object to that sort of thing not only in the clause under discussion but in other clauses of the bill which provide uneven benefits to taxpayers. My remarks apply even to the clause about which we talked previously, which one cannot mention at this time. That has been the pattern of this entire bill. Under this bill, the more you have got, the more you "gets", and the less you have got, the less you "gets". We object to that.

Mr. Chairman, generally I commend the changes being made. May I raise a question about the meaning of "prescribed information"? I am referring to those words appearing on line 27 of page 46 of the bill. A student attending an approved educational institution had to prove his attendance by filing with the minister a certificate of attendance from that educational institution. What does the minister intend in this regard? Why have the words "prescribed information" been included in subparagraph (g)?

As I understand the situation, Revenue Canada felt that a mere certificate of enrolment was not adequate. They wanted additional information as to the nature of courses, the period of time attended, and so on, for the purpose of making a judgment as to whether the individual person fitted within that category. That is my information.

Mr. Chairman, could I please have some information with regard to the new definition of "registered charity"? I am referring to page 47, subparagraph (4)(c). The amending paragraph reads in part, " ... and was either created or established in Canada." That provision did not exist in prior legislation.
There is, as a schedule to the Income Tax Act, a list of some 268 educational institutions, I think, known as universities outside Canada. They appear under Schedule I. Many Canadians have the advantage of an education at a university outside Canada, and from time to time they are asked to contribute to a foundation or scholarship program. Usually they are well disposed to make that contribution. After all, they have attended these institutions of learning, often at no expense to themselves, because they went on a scholarship. Frankly, I consider myself as one of them. We derived great benefit from our stay in those universities. Naturally, from time to time we

February 4, 1977
are called on to make contributions, either to a building fund or to a scholarship program.
In future, how will a Canadian resident or citizen who has attended one of these schools approved under Schedule I make a contribution, as a gift, to a charitable organization? In other words, the gift is truly to be considered as being made to a charitable organization. Does the present provision mean that we shall need to establish some foundation or what have you in Canada, which will collect these funds and then transmit them to the institution in question, whether in the United States or abroad?
I suppose the question is whether the hon. gentleman would make his contribution to Oxford University; I would make mine to Cambridge.
I would even allow you to do that.

In either case, the contribution is made directly to the institution, for example, to the trustees of Trinity Hall, Cambridge. The university itself will give me a receipt for that contribution. That, as I understand it, is not changed by the present provision. By way of comparison let me add that I believe that the Friends of Harvard University in Canada have a Canadian foundation to which funds are contributed; as a result of the contribution you get a receipt. As I understand it, under the new arrangement my hon. friend and I will still be able to make a trans-Atlantic contribution to an institution of learning. We will not have to make the contribution to a foundation in this country; but this provision has been introduced in case there is a foundation here.

Mr. Chairman, speaking about contributions to Oxford, it seems to me that there was an establishment in Toronto to which one sent contributions. That organization issued a receipt under the registered charities section. Unless one filed a receipt which had a registered number on it, the Minister of National Revenue would not recognize it. Therefore I could have sent thousands of pounds, if I had them, to my old college in the United Kingdom, but the Minister of National Revenue would not have recognized them.
Mr. Chairman, I could talk from other experience. I have sent contributions, not thousand of pounds, directly to my institution and received a receipt which has been allowed for tax purposes.
May I quote you?

By all means. I have to say that as one of those of my college in Canada interested in this question, I took the precaution of seeking advice from National Revenue in advance before I dunned everybody else to make a contribution. I believe that is in accordance with the law.

Mr. Chairman, this clause is presently under the guise of existing small business. The benefits being provided to small business are very substantial. The question is whether they are really going to small business rather than to the upper echelon, maybe a very small percentage of small business that in fact is not small business at all but verges on what I call much larger business, and these benefits are being provided under the guise that they will be of assistance to small business.
Rather than engage in an argument on this sort of thing, I would ask the minister for some figures that we could examine. The kinds of figures I would like from the minister include how many small businessmen there are in this country, how many of those small business companies pay any tax and, of that group of small businessmen, how many does the department anticipate would benefit from this kind of measure? Also, what is the cost to the federal treasury of this provision?
Mr. Chairman, I have to confess that I do not have instant responses to those four questions. I can seek them for the hon. member, but I do not have them at hand at the moment.

If we are being asked to pass a measure of this kind, that kind of information should be before the committee. As I started to say, it seems that the benefits really are not going to small business.
Just drawing on my memory of very old statistics, which are going to be approximate, and I put this before the committee with no more authority than to try to make a general point, the last time I looked at the figures, there were approximately 400,000 small businesses in Canada. Of that 400,000, over half paid no tax. They were not even in a taxable bracket, let alone being assisted by a measure of this kind. Of the other half, very few earned enough money to benefit from the provisions in any substantive way. The real beneficiaries of a clause of this kind are not small businessmen but some very substantial businesses which can well afford to pay the tax and do not need this kind of assistance.

On the final questions, Mr. Chairman, I can make an approximation. It is estimated that Canadian small business, however that may be defined, whether to the satisfaction of the hon. member or not, will save about $30 million in taxes in the first whole year.
(Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale).]
On the question raised by the hon. member as to how small is small, or when does small become medium or even large, to a degree the limits are set on the size by definitions already in the Income Tax Act. Without being precise in that regard, the hon. member and others can identify in their experience Canadian firms in particular which are in that middle ground without being able to carry on business with the contributed part of partners or subscribed capital of shareholders, and the very large businesses which are in the position to finance by a large public issue of shares.
There is a substantial number of companies in the centre, many of them Canadian owned, which are faced with the choice of either going out of business or selling the business to a going concern, primarily to a foreign party. One might argue that many of the takeovers which occurred in Canada in the past have had this transition difficulty, this financial difficulty which firms have run into. I do not pretend for a moment that this income measure is the complete answer to that problem, but it does seem to respond to a great deal of the concern Canadians have and, it seems to me, to a concern I have heard the hon. member himself mention from time to time, that Canadian controlled enterprises should have an opportunity to grow, and if that be our objective, as I take it to be, then some relief, at least from the standpoint of the corporate income tax burden, is one way of assisting in this respect.

It is the concern of this party that small business should grow to the extent possible, and it certainly is a concern of this party that as much of our business as possible be Canadian controlled. Nevertheless, I often think that many of the measures the government introduces in the guise of moving in this direction are perverse and misleading. It seems to me that the years in which we experienced the highest degree of foreign ownership were the years in which we had one of the most favourable tax systems in the western world. The favourableness of the tax system rather than the burden of taxation is what induced many businesses to sell out. We were the last country in the world to impose a capital gains tax, and when we did bring in such a measure it was only at half rates.
What was the consequence of not having a capital gains tax in Canada? The consequence, in my view, and I believe in the view of others who studied this question, was to encourage Canadian owners to sell their businesses, usually to American buyers rather than to Canadian buyers. The system works in that way. If you had a business and were working hard, you had to pay the regular rate of taxation. If you sold your business, without being liable for capital gains tax, you got a whopping sum of money which was totally exempt from taxation. The temptation to do so was incredible. Somebody would go to a businessman and say "Why are you working so hard? You are doing well and making money, but if you sell out you would do twice as well, because instead of having to pay tax on your earnings you would receive a capital amount and would not have to pay anything at all." That is one reason why so much of our industry sold out. It was not because the tax system was too harsh. It was because the tax system was
February 4, 1977

too biased in favour of selling out as against running at a profit.
To some extent the same situation prevails today with a 50 per cent capital gains tax in operation. The temptation is not so great but it still exists. It is still attractive to sell a business rather than run it, and this is really the problem. I believe a lot of things are wrong with our present system and that we have to assist Canadian business. But I do not think this provision will make any difference whatsoever.
What is interesting in observing the decisions which have come from FIRA is that this institution is in a box. It wants Canadian business to be bought out by Canadians, but there are very few Canadian buyers around to buy it out.
No wonder. They have no money. They are taxed to death.

That is the problem. There has been a failure to create institutions which can assist small business financially. One of the difficulties is the attitude of small businessmen themselves. They do not want to take in partners or put shares on the market; they want to own the whole thing themselves.
We have spoken in the House on a number of other occasions in favour of the Canada Development Corporation. We hoped we would have an instrument which would help Canadian business. Our argument was that instead of all these give-away programs through the tax system, the hidden welfare system, it would be better to take this money and turn it over to a venture company which would assist small business, go into partnership with small business, and help them with management, financing, merchandising on so on. This would do far more for Canadian business than these little bits and pieces, this shotgun approach by means of the tax system.
I am sure these measures do some good at some point. They are not totally lost. What I am suggesting is that so much is shot into the system that you do not know what does good and what does not do any good. The scatter gun approach is adopted simply because, after all, you have to do something. The government cannot be accused of not trying to help small business, of not being on the side of the little man, so it approves these measures which essentially help the bigger operator more than the smaller companies. The smaller operator really needs money not when he is making money; when you are making money you can usually get money. You have got credit by that time. You can get money from a bank or from investors. The problem for small businesses arises when they are not making money and when they do not benefit from measures of the kind proposed.
If the government really wants to assist small business it must provide assistance where it really counts. One way is by creating a venture capital company to help small business in every way possible. The other way is to help them when they are not paying tax rather than when they are paying tax. The worst possible way, and the least effective way of helping small business which is really small business, is through the measure which has been put before us this afternoon. I say this because the benefits of tax measures of this kind do not, in my
Pensions
experience, go to small businesses but to much larger businesses which are quite capable of looking after themselves.

My only comment is that it is high time that this provision was introduced. Notwithstanding what the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge has said, it represents a belated recognition by the government that we have experienced inflation for a number of years and that it is nonsense to keep things down at absolute figure maxima as they were in the act.

Clause agreed to.
Clauses 50 and 51 agreed to.
On Clause 52.

What was the rationale behind that change? Is an officially nominated candidate one who has been certified by the party leader to the chief electoral officer?

The explanation is this. Theoretically any individual might call himself or herself a candidate and commence issuing receipts to his or her supporters in return for political contributions. This is an attempt to bring the section a little closer within the framework of a formal political campaign.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED LOWERING OF AGE OF ELIGIBILITY, AND INCREASE IN BENEFITS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give consideration to the advisability of amending the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan to provide for the pensions payable under these two acts to be available at age 60 to all persons who meet the other requirements of the said acts and who are not in or are prepared to withdraw from the labour market, and also to provide for the basic amount of the pension payable under the Old Age Security Act, at age 60 for those not in the labour market and to everyone at age 65, to be increased to $250 per month, for this basic amount to be escalated each year by an amount that will enable pensioners not only to keep up with rising living costs but to share in rising living standards, and also to provide for the elimination of any means or income test from the Old Age Security Act, so that the full pension thereunder will be recognized as the established right of all our people.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I find it an interesting coincidence that this motion has been called for debate this afternoon. It so happens that yesterday when the government House leader was announcing the business for next week he indicated that one of the items to be called for second reading would be the government's bill, C-35, which is, in effect, an overhaul of the Old Age Security Act.
If I may underline what I mean about its being a coincidence, it arises from the fact that I shall be speaking in support of Bill C-35 when it comes before us. But I shall be indicating that there are two major shortcomings in Bill C-35. My motion deals with those two shortcomings. I hope the discussion we have this afternoon, and the discussion we will have on Bill C-35, might prompt the government, either at the second reading stage or in committee, to do something about these two shortcomings. One of these shortcomings has to do with the age at which pensions are available; the other has to do with the adequacy of the basic amount of old age security.
The first subject I wish to raise is that of the eligible age for pensions. I want to emphasize, even before I make my argument for lowering the age of eligibility, that what I am advocating-and advocating very strongly-is voluntaryism so far as early retirement is concerned.
I am not arguing that age 60 be the compulsory retirement age. However, I am arguing that the possibility of retiring at age 60 be available. If we are going to make that possibility real, I suggest we have to amend both the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan.
The minimum age for payments under these two pensions is still age 65 and in my experience there are a great many Canadians, particularly Canadians in industry, who find the "rat race" very hard these days, and who feel that they ought to have the opportunity of retiring at age 60 instead age 65.
If we could persuade the government to make old age security available at age 60 that would be a good step, a partial step. If we were to make both old age security and Canada Pension Plan benefits available at age 60 many persons would be able to take advantage of that. However, as my motion suggests, that in itself would not be everybody.
February 4, 1977

The fact that I am emphasizing voluntaryism is underlined by the words in my motion that state pensions should be available under the two acts to persons at age 60 who are out of the labour market. I propose that there be no means test between ages 60 and 65. I wish also to emphasize there should be no marital test as there is with respect to the spouses' allowances that are now available.
A pension to those between the ages of 60 and 65 who are out of the labour market would take care of the spouses of pensioners, or of those at home whose spouses are working. It would also take care of spinsters and widows, bachelors and widowers who are not now covered by the spouse's allowance.
In the 1974 election campaign when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) first announced that the government would bring in a spouse's allowance I distinctly remember hearing him say that this would create problems. It has created problems. The main problem is that it does not cover a great many individuals. There is the horrible problem that arises where a spouse between the ages of 60 and 65 may get the spouse's allowance because he or she is living with a spouse who is of pensionable age, then a year or so later the older spouse dies when the younger spouse has not yet reached the age of 65, therefore, the younger spouse loses the allowance.
The figures we have from the department indicate that this is affecting approximately 200 individual Canadians every month. The Prime Minister was right during the 1974 election campaign when he said this would create problems as well as solve problems. I think the problems should now be solved by extending pensions to persons between the ages of 60 and 65 who are out of the labour market. I use that phrase to cover both those who are already out of the labour market because they are at home, or whatever, and those who voluntarily leave the labour market.
I am quite sympathetic to the arguments made by some about the difficulties of a fixed pension age. Speeches to that effect have been made in this House, and may again be made today. Studies made on this issue, particularly one under the aegis of the Canadian Council on Social Development raise this whole question of whether or not we should have a fixed age at which people must retire, and I go along with the proposition, that it should not be fixed, it should not be compulsory. My motion does not ask for compulsory retirement. My motion asks for the possibility of retirement at age 60. That would be possible if the old age security pension and the retirement benefits under the Canada Pension Plan were made available at that age.
I know what happens to private members' resolutions in private members' hours. I do not see any reason to hope that the same thing will not happen to mine this afternoon, but I hope that the discussion we will have today will have some bearing on the debate next week and on the debate when we get into committee on the government's Bill C-35.
The other phase of the motion that is now before the House is to the effect that the basic amount of old age security should
Pensions
be increased to at least S250 a month. There are organizations and persons in Canada who will say that that figure is not high enough. I have seen resolutions for a much higher figure and I go along with them, but in this House one has to move a step at a time, and since the basic amount of old age security is at present $141.34 a month, perhaps I am asking for all I dare ask for, namely, that it be increased by about $109 to $250 a month. I am still opposed to the means test concept that attaches to the guaranteed income supplement. We have been over that battle many a time and I do not wish to take time on it this afternoon, but at the moment at any rate there are amounts available on top of the present basic pension which bring the total that an individual and a married couple can reach up to a certain figure. But these figures are still very inadequate, and even though it is a time of restraint, a time when some persons will say we have done enough for pensioners, let us leave that subject alone, I insist that our older people have the right to have their plight considered.
I hold in my hand a clipping from the Ottawa Citizen of Tuesday, January 4, 1977, with a Canadian Press dispatch from Toronto under the heading, "Elderly Need Up to $695 Each Month". This story is based on a report put out by the Social Planning Council of Metropolitan Toronto, funded by the Department of National Health and Welfare. The figures in this report suggest that a couple in Toronto today, if that couple owns its own home, needs at least $654 to get by. On the other hand, if that couple has to rent accommodation, it needs at least $695 a month to get by. I have looked at the details making up those figures and in a number of cases it seems to me that the figures are very conservative. These totals of $654 a month for a couple owning their own home and $695 for a couple having to rent are certainly minimal.
In defence of the proposal I make which would add about $109 a month to the basic pension now being paid, may I say that even if my motion were passed and everyone received the full $250 a month which my motion proposes and, on top of that, the full amount that is now being paid as a supplement, the totals would still be a little below these minimal amounts that have been given to us by the Social Planning Council of Metropolitan Toronto.
I urge that this matter be given serious consideration. I know that there have been times in this parliament when the mood and the climate were such that one could push for better benefits for senior citizens and make more headway than one could at other times. I know that at the moment it is a rather hostile time, with all the preaching about restraint and all the rest of it. But the fact of the matter is that the nearly 2 million Canadians who are 65 years of age or over have a right to have their conditions improved, and I think it is little enough to ask that the basic pension for these persons be fixed at not less than $250 a month plus the additions that are provided in the legislation.
Now, Sir, there are many aspects to this. There is the whole question of escalation, the question of universality, taxation, and other things in which senior citizens are interested.

We have moved a long way since I first started talking about old age pensions in this place. We have moved into the field of housing, of medicare, and so on. but it is still true that at least half of the Canadian people who are 65 years of age and over are having a tough time to get along, and we should do a lot better for them.

I present the motion, hoping that this time the House will consider it favourably.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my contribution to the debate on this motion will be as brief as possible; however, first of all I want to congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for the motion he has placed before the House. We must recognize that the dean of the House is demonstrating considerable perseverance while taking advantage of every means offered by the procedure to urge the government to improve the lot of each and every Canadian 60 years old and over, something for which the House should commend him.
On the other hand, the platform of the Social Credit Party of Canada, to which I belong, has always included a provision for lowering the optional retirement age limit to 60. Therefore, not only do we advocate lowering retirement age, but we urge the government to increase the amounts paid under the Old Age Security Pension and the Canada Pension Plan so that all retired Canadians may have enough to support themselves.
Is Canada economically and financially able to meet the requirements of this motion? The gross national product is kept at a reasonable rate, in spite of the increase in the number of unemployed Canadians. They could help increase the GNP if they could use their energies to make the production greater, thus allowing us to reach quite easily the aim of the motion.
Financially, we also can wonder whether Canada can face such expenditures. As far as I am concerned, I think so, but budgetary cuts should obviously be made, especially with respect to the interest paid by Canada on the national debt. In the current fiscal year, the federal treasury will have to pay $4 billion; interest on the national debt alone and it is impossible to know from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) to whom that interest is paid. Let me refer to the answer reported in Hansard for February 1, 1977 in reply to a question I raised, No. 1,389. I was asking for some information every Canadian should know, namely the total amount of the national debt, to whom is this debt owing and who are our creditors. Is this a long term or a short term debt? Efforts will be made

to try to find answers which are not available. Interests are paid, but we cannot know to whom? We owe money and we do not know to whom?
I believe the Minister of Finance should consider the answer that has been given, and I imagine it was prepared by a public servant who did not want to take the trouble of going to the bottom of things. I do not know the public servant who prepared the answer, but I know the Minister of Finance well, and this is why I ask him to do everything possible to provide us with information on this matter because we are entitled to it. We should know the true financial situation of our country.
From the reply it has given, the government is obviously not prepared, as I have just said, to give us this information, but once again, I demand it. The government is able to tell us to whom we have paid $2,975,787,998 for the old age security pension of people 65 and over. It is able to provide us with names and addresses and it is also able to tell the House that an amount of $34,936,432 was paid out in allocations to the spouses 60 and over from October 1975 to March 31, 1976. It can also tell the House that the amount of $923,251,220 was paid out in income supplement, which makes a total of $3,933,975,630. The government is able to provide all this information to the House. I congratulate the government because those are clear answers that have been read into the official report.
Mr. Speaker, as of April 1, 1976, there were 855,600 males and 1,101,300 females aged 65 and over, or a total of 1,956,900 people who received old age security pensions. I am putting all those Figures on the record in answer to those who suggest that it is impossible, that the expense is beyond our means. And when I am finished with those figures, I believe it will be recognized that the motion now before us is reasonable and Canada can afford it.
At the same date, there were 896,900 people between 60 and 64 years, 434,900 males and 462,000 females. We would have to know how many are now receiving spouse allowances, in order to know how many would be entitled to OAS pensions and to determine the actual cost to the federal treasury. That could be computed. Of the total cost, deduction should be made of the current cost to the federal treasury of social welfare benefits paid to people in that category under agreements with the provinces. The actual cost would be known only after such computations were made.
There is another factor to consider. A number of those people will retire voluntarily from the labour force, to be replaced mainly by people currently unemployed who now receive government assistance in the form of unemployment insurance or social welfare benefits. This involves a significant amount of money. If those unemployed were to take the jobs vacated by people retiring, this would mean so much UIC and welfare benefits we would not have to pay. Moreover, these new wage earners will be paying taxes that will replete the federal treasury and help pay the OAS benefits referred to in this motion.
February 4, 1977

For all these reasons it is high time in my view that the government introduce legislation to amend existing acts, to give such persons the benefits referred to in the motion.
1 suggest this country must secure a well deserved income security for elderly people. If we consider all achievements in Canada over the past 40 years, one can see they are largely due to people who are 60 years or over, keeping in mind nevertheless that younger ones have also contributed.
One must also take into account that people of 60 and over have worked in very difficult and sometimes inhuman conditions and that without their courage and strength, today's generation would not have the facilities and opportunities now at their disposal. By the way, Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask young people and adults who are or would like to be on the labour market to talk to elderly people and draw comparisons between opportunities today and at that time. At present, one can load a van while sitting on a heavy machine and handling levers, whereas people of 60 years and over had to do it with small shovels with handles three feet long. It was much more exhausting and much less profitable. Young people, who crit-ize easily, should absolutely consider all the advantages of which they can avail themselves. I am convinced they can reason and take all these matters into consideration. They would surely be willing to pay more taxes to ensure old age security pensions at a reasonable rate and enable elderly people to enjoy for a few more years the opportunities Canada may offer them.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, we must be grateful to the hon. member and we should adopt this motion as soon as possible. We would then show much understanding and would at the same time carry out our duty as parliamentarians and administrators.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with pensions being So prominent in the news, particularly with regard to indexing, I am very pleased to be able to speak today on motion No. 23. The reputation of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is well known and respected, particularly in the area of pension plans, and for that reason I should like to be able to assure him of my support for this motion.

speechtext: At least the hon. member's heart is in the right place.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED LOWERING OF AGE OF ELIGIBILITY, AND INCREASE IN BENEFITS
speechtext:
However, that is not possible because, far from improving the situation with regard to pension plans in Canada, this motion might in some ways and in some cases make the situation even worse.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has made a number of suggestions in his motion which would represent a radical change in the Canadian pension system and in the costs paid by the Canadian taxpayer. Before looking at these proposals in detail, I think it might be useful to look at the present system of pensions in Canada, to consider the many changes and improvements which have been made in the old age
Pensions
security program and the Canada Pension Plan, and to examine the benefits retired Canadians can expect under the current provisions of these programs. Such an examination appears to be in order if an objective assessment is to be made of the sweeping alterations proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Just 12 years ago, in 1965, the income guaranteed to a retired Canadian by the government of Canada was only $75 per month, payable at age 70 under the Old Age Security Act. In other words, a married couple both 70 years of age or over could expect a total of $ 1,800 per year only, in public pensions. If they wished to retire at an earlier age or live at a higher standard it was expected they would have private resources to do so. Since then some dramatic improvements have been made in retirement benefits for the elderly.
In 1966 the retirement age for old age security began to be reduced, a year at a time, until it reached the present old age security retirement age of 65 in 1970. This fact should be borne clearly in mind when looking at suggestions to reduce retirement age to 60. The payment of OAS benefits as early as age 65 has been available for only seven years.
Also in 1966 the Canada Pension Plan came into effect. This compulsory and contributory pension plan, which covers virtually every Canadian wage earner, has grown increasingly important as a source of present and future retirement income. The maximum new CPP retirement benefit payable in 1977 is $173.61 per month, and consequently exceeds the current Old Age Security benefit of $141.34 per month.
Two points underlying the introduction of the Canada Pension Plan and most relevant to this motion should perhaps be made at this juncture. The first is that the Canada Pension Plan was designed as a pension scheme whose ultimate retirement benefit would be related to the contributor's lifetime earnings, and which would be funded by the contributions of its membership. It was realized that living costs vary greatly between urban and rural areas as well as between different regions in Canada. The income which Canadian people needed, if either retirement, death or disability of the head of the family were to remove the regular source of income, was related in part to the level of earnings to which they had become accustomed. Thus, what underlay the creation of the Canada Pension Plan was an understanding that adequate levels of pension could not realistically be achieved in a country like Canada simply by increasing the flat rate OAS pension indefinitely. That understanding is equally applicable today in considering this motion.
The second point that should be made about the Canada Pension Plan is that it was not intended to provide all the retirement income which Canadians might wish to have, even in conjunction with the Old Age Security pension. Rather, the Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act were seen as providing the first two layers in a three-tiered retirement system. The first tier, the fiat rate Old Age Security pension, provides a base on which the second tier, the earnings related

Canada and Quebec Pension Plan benefits, is built. Together with the guaranteed income supplement, these benefits ensure a minimum amount of income which adequately provides for the basic needs of the individual on retirement. The third level of the system is the additional income available through private pension plans, registered retirement savings plans, investments or other sources, which can be seen as providing whatever supplementary margin of comfort the individual might require.
The suggestion that Old Age Security benefits be raised to $250 should therefore not be looked on as a recommendation that Canadian pensioners should be provided with a retirement income of $250 per month. Rather, it is a recommendation that the over-all benefits for pensioners from a three-tiered system of retirement income should be increased, by an amount which would vary between about only $10 and $110. This variation, by the way, comes as a result of the suggestion in the motion that the other income support programs embodied in the OAS program be dropped. These income support programs are the guaranteed income supplement and the spouses' allowance.
The guaranteed income supplement, or GIS, was introduced in 1967 very shortly after the Canada Pension Plan came into being. The maximum benefit under this program was originally set at $30 per month during the first year of the program and 40 per cent of the OAS pension for subsequent years. An income test was applied to the benefits, and provided for reductions of $1 for every $2 of extra income, excluding Old Age Security benefits for a single person. For a married couple the reduction was $1 for every $4 of family income.
GIS was originally intended to be a transitional program which would gradually be phased out as the Canada Pension Plan took effect. The supplement was therefore made available only to persons born before December 31, 1910, that is, to persons who were over 55 years of age at the inception of the CPP and who would therefore not have an opportunity to build a full ten-year CPP benefit before reaching age 65.
It was felt that those who did have an opportunity to build a full CPP retirement pension would have less need for such a supplementation program. However, in practice this has not proved to be entirely the case. Some persons, housewives, for example, are not directly covered by the Canada Pension Plan or only become entitled to a small CPP pension on retirement. The guaranteed income supplement proved to be of great value in providing income only for those retired Canadians who were most in need, without placing an inordinate burden on the Canadian taxpayer. Consequently the supplement was made permanent in 1970, and since then has been expanded and improved. The maximum GIS benefit is now $99.13 per month, which is more than 70 per cent of the current Old Age Pension.
I should emphasize the value of this program, since it is implicit in the motion which we are discussing that the guaranteed income supplement would be eradicated and, in effect, replaced by a very large increase in the flat rate OAS benefit. The replacement will cost vastly more, and will mainly benefit
[Mr. Philbrook.j
those whose income is already large enough that they do not qualify for a substantial amount of supplementation. I would note that the suggested benefit level would raise the income of a single person now receiving the full supplement, by less than $10. Such a pensioner already receives $240.47 per month as of January 1, 1977. With the pension being indexed, this may well go over $250 in the near future.
It is clear that the member's proposal fails to bridge the income gap between those who depend on OAS benefits and those who have other means. On the contrary, a retired Canadian who formerly received the guaranteed income supplement would suddenly find that his income, relative to that of other pensioners with large CPP or private pensions, has dropped sharply. The existence of GIS has, in effect, been a recognition that those who had no opportunity to contribute to CPP have made a contribution, perhaps in other ways. We should not be overly hasty in removing this recognition simply in order to provide some pensioners with more money.

Mr. Speaker, I would prefer to leave it to the end, if I may. I have only a few more remarks to finish off.
These remarks would apply equally to the spouse's allowance, which is also an income tested benefit, and which was made a part of the old age security program in 1975. The spouse's allowance provides a benefit for spouses, between the ages of 60 and 65, of persons in receipt of old age security benefits. The maximum amount of the spouse's allowance is equal to the basic old age security benefit plus the maximum guaranteed income supplement at the married rate.
This program, like the guaranteed income supplement, was introduced in recognition of the special needs of a particularly vulnerable segment of the retired population. Married couples are more often than not several years apart in age. Consequently, it will often happen that the major or only wage earner in the family will reach age 65 and retire, or be forced to retire, but the spouse, being several years younger, is not yet entitled to OAS or GIS benefits. This situation meant that many retired couples were having to struggle along for several years on a single old age security pension and a single guaranteed income supplement payment before the other spouse finally became eligible for OAS and GIS benefits.
On the other hand, many couples are not placed in financial difficulty through differences in their ages. We can imagine, for instance, a family with a single wage-earner where the spouse who works at home has reached age 65, while the wage-earner is several years younger and is still working. This couple has not retired in any sense of the word and should not be given any special benefits. It is for reasons such as this that benefits like the spouse's allowance are income-tested.
February 4, 1977

To show what can happen with an inflexible and monolithic approach we could imagine for the moment that the suggestions made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre have been adopted in full. Suppose now that the major wage-earner in the family reaches age 60 and retires. Again this may very well be a compulsory retirement, if past experience with lowering retirement ages is any indication. If the spouse at home is a few years younger, we have recreated the same problem five years earlier. The government of the day would have the alternatives of ignoring the same very serious problem which this government felt it could not disregard, or of reintroducing the income-tested spouse's allowance, payable now at age 55. Therefore you are back to square one.
With the introduction of the spouse's allowance, the current spectrum of public retirement pension programs is virtually complete. However, there are a number of major benefit improvements which have also occurred in the past few years which are relevant to this motion.
May I mention them briefly, without going into detail? I am thinking of measures for indexing OAS and CPP introduced in 1967. These programs have been indexed quarterly since 1973. I think also of the periodic quantum jumps in these benefits which took place in 1970, 1972 and 1973 and of the elimination of qualifying tests with regard to CPP in 1975. As the minister has announced, the government plans to introduce a new bill providing for reciprocal agreements with other countries for pension plans and payments.
As a result of the many improvements in benefits for the aged in recent years, some of which I have described, the elderly are now guaranteed income levels which often exceed those guaranteed to other deserving groups such as the disabled, the retarded, certain single parent families, and the working poor. Could we in all conscience direct the very large amounts of additional funds which these proposals would entail entirely toward increasing benefits to the elderly, without considering whether, with the limited resources available for income security, we should not be directing our attention to the needs of these other groups?
In closing, may I congratulate the hon. member on introducing this motion for debate.

Mr. Speaker, I would not deny for a moment the figures brought forward relating to need. I am not arguing that point, but I am glad he raised it. That is why it was doubly incumbent for some spokesman on the government side to indicate why the hon. member's proposal cannot be adopted. But this has not happened.
I suggest that not one member of this House would say that if the figures proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre are reasonably attainable, those amounts ought not to be paid to senior citizens of this country. But some members skirt round the issue. Some regurgitate ministerial speeches; some read answers to questions on the order paper. But I suggest that not one member of this House would say that we ought not to pay that amount if it could be established that, as a country, we can afford to pay it.
The hon. member's case must be made or rejected, otherwise this kind of debate degenerates to an auction, to a tendering contest.
Some further considerations deserve mentioning. I do not know if the $250 figure is right, if it ought to be $300, or more, or less. I do not know that; that is why I listened carefully to the debate in this House. I wanted to hear someone say that that figure is wrong. Yet nobody on the government side said that. I suggest that, in the face of the need demonstrated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, if the figure he mentioned is attainable, it ought to be paid. But it is important not to let this kind of debate degenerate into an auction.
We ought to address ourselves to the problems of this country's senior citizens, because there are problems. I talked

Pensions
on the telephone yesterday to a senior citizen who says that the pension base is too low. Our older people say, "We like indexing; it is fine, but the figure upon which indexing is based is too low." Senior citizens are in favour of indexing. Some think it is wonderful. Although some of them deny it, I suggest that indexing is a great benefit for senior citizens. Yet, as I say, the base is low. They come to me and say, "Mr. Baker, I cannot pay my rent; I cannot pay the fuel bill; I am a proud person; I do not want to go on welfare." They say this to all of us in this House. I am sure that hon. members who represent senior citizens know that this is the case, that I am correct in saying these things.
All in this House applauded when we recently increased the Canada Pension Plan pay out. What happened when we increased that pay out? That increase was necessary by virtue of the ravages of inflation. I do not intend to sound partisan, because our inflation was out of control. No sooner had we granted an increase in the Canada Pension Plan than the provincial governments lopped off from their contributions an amount equal to the increase we had brought forward. Provincial departments responsible for social affairs put people back into positions they had previously occupied when they had suffered from the ravages of inflation running at 10 per cent, or more per annum. That is something we in parliament must attack if we are to walk out of this place with our heads high. We should be able to tell our constituents that we are doing something for the disadvantaged.
Why are we in politics? All of us, regardless of what side of the House we sit on, are here because we are concerned one way or another. Everyone of us wants this country to be a place where a senior citizen or a person approaching that age can have a sense of security. They do not now have a sense of security. It is better than it was, but they do not have it. Anyone who goes among senior citizens knows this.
We want this country to be for senior citizens just as we want it to be the land of opportunity for young people. We do not want our young people to be satisfied with the lowest common denominator. Surely we ought not to allow our senior citizens to be satisfied with the lowest common denominator either. There are some real challenges to us in social services legislation, not only in dollar terms but in the integration of that legislation. There is not a member of this House who does not support the spirit in which this has been advanced.
I want to say something else to the hon. member. I know he emphasized at the beginning of his speech the aspect of voluntariness in terms of retiring. He knows and I know, because we have discussed it, that there is bound to be in any system, even based on a voluntary acceptance of it, an encouragement to people to opt out of their professions and jobs because there is an opportunity for them to do so. I would not deny them that opportunity, but I think there can be a denial of their expertise, training and wisdom to the country. The country needs them.
My father, who died a year ago on March 5, was a druggist in a small town. My mother, my brother and I tried to

persuade him to stop working because he was getting old. He said to me, "What would I do? I could work in my garden for a while. I could look after my wife, but how am I going to stay in the mainstream of life? Who is it that can face me and encourage me to leave the mainstream of life?" That is what we may be doing with this motion. We finally talked him into selling his small business. The only term and condition upon which he would sell was if his nephew, who bought it, would allow him to work in it. He worked out his days until he was stricken and died, but he contributed.
In many ways we are looking at the wrong end of this spectrum. We ought to be encouraging people to work. We let judges sit until they are 75, and very few of them retire before that time. Why? Because they have something to contribute.
I went to a senior citizen's meeting at the Nepean Sport-splex. Good friends of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre were there. We discussed the problem of how to involve them in the community in a big way. The hon. member's good friends, and he knows who I am talking about, came to me and said that they want to be involved.
I looked over that group. There were retired statisticians, businessmen, professional men, teachers, nurses, all people who want to contribute. We have come to the point where we look for people going out of the work force instead of working and searching for policies that will widen the opportunities for people to go into the work force. We sometimes see the wrong end of the problem.
I do not want the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to feel that I oppose his motion, because I do not.
